title: Bailey explains why stronger growth can coexist with spare capacity across the UK
summary: Andrew Bailey defended the November quarter-point increase in Bank Rate to 4% while explaining why the next decision remains open. Higher energy prices had already pushed UK inflation to 3.6% in October. The Bank’s November projection put inflation at around 5% by the middle of 2027, before the energy contribution faded and restrictive policy weighed on prices. Evidence of higher energy costs spreading to other prices and wages was still limited. Bailey judged the pressure already in the pipeline sufficient for the November increase. His conditional warning was about duration: the longer energy prices remained elevated, the greater the risk of lasting inflation and the higher rates might need to be.

The growth surprise changed the context for that judgement. The Bank expected GDP to grow by around 1.6% in 2026, up from just over 1% in the summer. Private activity, particularly business services, had supplied most of the resilience. That differed from the larger role of public output over the previous three years. Stronger international activity had supported UK exports and manufacturing. Real incomes had supported consumption, although consumer confidence had dropped back and higher energy bills and mortgage rates were expected to weigh on spending. Spare capacity remained in the labour market, but its margin appeared to have stopped widening as growth picked up.

An experimental staff measure attributed just under a fifth of GDP growth so far that year to new AI-related activity. The denominator is growth over the period. The estimate describes neither a fifth of the level of UK output nor an economy-wide productivity gain. Bailey stressed the measurement uncertainty and said the activity was concentrated in technology investment and capital deepening. Evidence of gains from wider adoption was still modest. The distinction matters for inflation. Additional spending can support demand relatively quickly, whereas diffusion of more productive techniques may take time and differ across sectors and regions.

The regional evidence separates the productivity of people in work from the share of people participating. In 2023 London’s output per hour exceeded the UK average by 28.5%, while the North West recorded the fastest annual growth in output per hour between 2019 and 2023, at an average 2.4%. A slower-growing region can still have a higher level of productivity. Labour-market indicators also need to be read together. In July to September Northern Ireland recorded unemployment of 2.2% alongside inactivity of 25.8% and employment of 72.5%. Low measured unemployment can coexist with many people outside the labour force.

Bailey connected these differences to how new investment reaches the rest of a local economy. A cluster can attract productive businesses while transport, housing or shortages of relevant skills limit access to the jobs it creates. Local supply chains and links with universities can help gains spread. The Bank’s 12 regional agencies hold about 6,000 discussions with contacts each year, providing evidence on costs, demand and staffing alongside national statistics. That intelligence helps the MPC judge how a common energy shock affects an industry-intensive area compared with a service centre. The speech gives one national inflation objective and no estimate of how much additional UK output any particular regional initiative would produce.

questions.question: Which evidence would show that the energy shock is starting to persist in UK prices?
questions.detail: Bailey sees pressure in the pipeline but limited evidence of spillovers into wages and other prices. The next rate decision depends partly on whether that assessment changes. Compare the next official wage and services-price releases with the Bank’s Agents’ accounts of pay settlements, pricing plans and the extent to which firms absorb costs. Look for broadening pressure across less energy-intensive sectors as well as direct increases in energy bills.

questions.question: How much of the AI-related growth reflects spending today versus higher productive capacity?
questions.detail: The staff proxy assigns a significant share of this year’s growth to new activity, while Bailey says wider productivity gains remain modest and measurement is uncertain. Those mechanisms have different implications for margins, inflation and rates. Consult detailed investment and industry output data, then compare equipment spending with output per hour and evidence from adopters, allowing time for new capital to affect production.

questions.question: Where could additional investment draw people into employment rather than compete for an already employed workforce?
questions.detail: The speech distinguishes high inactivity from unemployment and highlights local transport, housing and skills constraints. A business estimating hiring costs needs to know whether workers can reach its site and fill the jobs offered. Combine regional employment and inactivity estimates with local skills and commuting evidence. The Bank’s regional contacts can help interpret the survey estimates and identify differences within a single region.

limitation: The staff estimate of AI-related activity is an uncertain proxy. Regional labour-market indicators use different denominators, and the address gives no predetermined rate path.
